text: One closing worked scenario, pulling every chapter of this course into a single argument — and a last chance to size a real system end to end, honestly.

Chapter 1 established the problem: real qubits decohere and suffer gate errors, which is why hardware can't just run longer to get reliable answers. Chapter 2 showed why the classical fix doesn't transfer: you can't measure a qubit without collapsing it, and no-cloning forbids copying an unknown state. Chapter 3 built the real mechanism: entanglement instead of copying, and syndrome measurement that reveals the error but never the data — the bit-flip and phase-flip codes, and Shor's nine-qubit code combining both into the first proof quantum error correction is possible at all. Chapter 4 generalized this into the stabilizer formalism and the CSS construction, producing the Steane seven-one-three code — the same single-error protection, fewer physical qubits, and transversal gates as a bonus.

Chapter 5 showed why the surface code, not Steane or Shor, is the leading practical candidate: nearest-neighbor-only connectivity, a comparatively favorable threshold, and low-weight local stabilizers, at the cost of a much larger but tunable physical-qubit overhead. Chapter 6 quantified that overhead precisely and paired it with the threshold theorem's promise — below threshold, each step up in distance buys exponentially better suppression for only quadratically more qubits. Chapter 7 closed the gap between having a code and having a fault-tolerant computer: fault-tolerant gadgets, magic-state distillation for the one gate transversal tricks can't provide, and an honest accounting of where real hardware stands today.

Suppose you're asked to size a system for 50 logical qubits, each protected at distance 21. Using the verified surface-code formula, the per-logical-qubit cost is 2 times 441 minus 1, or 881 physical qubits. Fifty logical qubits times 881 gives 44,050 physical qubits, just for the base error-correcting code, before adding any magic-state distillation overhead. None of this materializes unless the hardware's actual error rate sits below the surface code's threshold. And 44,050 qubits, before distillation, is far beyond any current NISQ-era device.

This single scenario is the whole course in miniature: the theory says scaling up is worth it, the arithmetic says exactly what it costs, and the honest assessment says current hardware isn't there yet — all three true at once. Holding all three together, rather than collapsing into either 'it's hopeless' or 'it's basically solved,' is the real, defensible professional position in this field today. That's the course.
